title: Things around you: the ki-/vi- class and demonstratives
goal: Name the things around you, haggle a little at a craft market, and point precisely: this, that, and the one over there.
bekal: the *ki-/vi-* class: *kitabu → vitabu*, and adjectives that follow its prefix
three kinds of demonstratives: *hiki* (this), *hicho* (that one mentioned), *kile* (that one far away)
how to read the sound of a prefix to guess the demonstrative of any class

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sokoni la vitu vya mikono
dialogs.intro: The craft market in Stone Town. Budi is looking for a gift for his sister, with Amina along.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Hiki ni kikapu cha mkono. Watu hapa wanatengeneza vikapu vizuri.
lines.id: This is a handmade basket. People here make beautiful baskets.
lines.literal: this-thing is basket of hand. people here they-are-making baskets good-ones.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ni kizuri sana! Na hivi ni nini?
lines.id: It's very nice! And what are these?
lines.literal: is good-one very! and these-things are what?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Hivi ni viatu vya ngozi. Vinatoka Mombasa.
lines.id: These are leather shoes. They come from Mombasa.
lines.literal: these-things are shoes of leather. they-are-coming-from Mombasa.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Hapana, ni rahisi. Shilingi elfu kumi tu.
lines.id: No, they're cheap. Only ten thousand shillings.
lines.literal: no, is easy. shilling thousand ten only.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kitu gani ni kizuri kwa dada yangu?
lines.id: What would be a good thing for my sister?
lines.literal: thing which is good for sister of-me?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Kikapu hiki kidogo ni kizuri. Au vikombe hivi.
lines.id: This little basket is nice. Or these cups.
lines.literal: basket this small is good. or cups these.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Ni vinne. Vyote ni vya udongo.
lines.id: There are four. They're all clay.
lines.literal: are four. all-of-them are of clay.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I like that black one over there!

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Kile ni kizuri kabisa. Bei yake ni elfu tano.
lines.id: That one is really beautiful. Its price is five thousand.
lines.literal: that-thing is good completely. price of-it is thousand five.

notes: **Kitu means "thing" and Swahili uses it as often as English uses "thing" or "stuff".** *Kitu gani?* (what thing?), *kitu kimoja* (one thing), *hakuna kitu* (nothing). The plural is *vitu*.

**Vya, cha mean "of; made of".** The form follows the class of the noun: *kikapu cha mkono* (hand basket), *viatu vya ngozi* (leather shoes), *vikombe vya udongo* (clay cups). You've already met its cousins in unit 2: *picha ya familia*, *watoto wa kaka*.

**Ghali and rahisi never change form.** Both are Arabic loans, so they don't follow a class: *kitabu ghali*, *nyumba ghali*, *viatu ghali*. Other loan adjectives that behave the same: *safi* (clean), *tayari* (ready), *muhimu* (important), *bora* (best), *hodari* (clever; hard-working).

**Rahisi means both "cheap" and "easy".** It has two opposites: *ghali* for prices, *gumu* for difficulty. If someone says *Kiswahili ni rahisi*, they are saying this language is easy — and so far they're not wrong.

**Cheusi is ki- + eusi.** The prefix *ki-* turns into *ch-* before a vowel: *ki + eusi* → *cheusi* (black), *ki + eupe* → *cheupe* (white), and *ki + ingi* → *vingi* for the plural. A small sound rule that applies throughout this class.

grammars.title: The ki-/vi- class — handmade things
body: The second class you set up holds mostly **man-made things**: tools, furniture, implements. Singular **ki-**, plural **vi-** — and as usual, adjectives and numbers change along.
after: The last two rows show the sound rule: **ki- becomes ch- and vi- becomes vy- before a vowel**. *Ki + akula* → *chakula*. *Vi + akula* → *vyakula*. Words like *chumba*, *choo* (toilet) and *chuo* (college) are really members of this class in disguise.

The prefix *ki-* is also a word-making machine. It marks **languages**: *Kiswahili*, *Kiingereza*, *Kiindonesia*. It marks **manner**: *kienyeji* (in the local way), *kizungu* (Western style). And it makes things smaller: *mtoto* (child) → *kitoto* (tiny baby), *kijiji* (small village) from *mji* (town).
The *vi-* before an adjective produces the adverbs you've used since unit 3: *vizuri* (well), *vibaya* (badly), *vingi* (a lot), *vipi?* (how?).

grammars.title: This, that, and the one over there
body: Swahili distinguishes **three** distances, not two. English has "this" and "that"; Swahili adds a third for something that has just been mentioned in the conversation.
after: There is a pattern that saves you the whole table. The "this" demonstrative is built from **h + the vowel of the class prefix + the class prefix**: class *ki-* → *h* + *i* + *ki* = **hiki**. Class *vi-* → *h* + *i* + *vi* = **hivi**. Class *wa-* → *h* + *a* + *wa* = **hawa**. Once you hear the pattern, you don't need to memorize the table.

The "that (just mentioned)" forms (*hicho*, *hiyo*, *hayo*) are used for something **already mentioned in the conversation**, even if the thing is right in front of you. These are the most common in everyday talk: *Hiyo ni kweli* — "That's true" (what you just said).

The demonstrative stands **after** its noun: *kitabu hiki* (this book), *watu hawa* (these people). Put it in front — *hiki kitabu* — and the meaning shifts to emphasis: "**this** book, not that one".

sections.title: Vitu ndani ya chumba — what's in the room

blocks.text: Note that not all of these belong to the *ki-/vi-* class. *Meza*, *taa* and *sahani* are loanwords in the *nyumba* class (unit 7); *mlango* is in the *mti* class (unit 16); *dirisha* and *sanduku* are in the *gari* class (unit 9). This course sets up the classes one at a time, so for now just memorize the plural forms as they are.

sections.title: Rangi — colors, and the ones that change prefix

blocks.text: Colors fall into two groups, and the difference matters because only the first group changes prefix to match its noun.

To ask: *Rangi gani?* (what color?). The answer can use *ni* or not: *Kitabu ni cheusi* or *kitabu cheusi* (a black book). Notice *kijani* (green) — literally "like a leaf", from *jani* (leaf); and *kahawia* (brown) — from *kahawa* (coffee).
